content: The survey protocol must undergo a thorough review by an ethics review committee or a research review committee before its implementation. If the survey is funded by the World Health Organization (WHO), it is mandatory to obtain approval from the WHO Research Ethics Review Committee. The survey must be conducted strictly in accordance with the approved protocol. Countries are required to establish robust quality control and quality assurance measures for laboratory procedures. WHO provides prequalified laboratory-based enzyme immunoassays and rapid diagnostic tests for detecting hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg). A list of WHO-prequalified tests is available on the WHO website. If countries opt to use other assays, the sensitivity and specificity of these assays must be evaluated. WHO may assist in proficiency testing of such assays or retesting of selected specimens. Surveys utilizing rapid tests with validated sensitivity and specificity are acceptable for verification purposes. Rapid tests offer several advantages, including lower costs, minimal or no need for laboratory infrastructure or cold chain systems, and the requirement of only a small volume of blood (a few drops). Certain rapid tests can be performed using capillary blood obtained via fingerstick, thereby eliminating the need for venipuncture. It is essential to follow the manufacturer’s instructions regarding acceptable specimen types and volumes. As of December 2019, seven test products have been prequalified by WHO, including two rapid tests. The WHO list of prequalified in vitro diagnostic products is accessible online. Countries seeking verification of hepatitis B control through immunization must prepare a comprehensive verification package. This includes a completed verification report, data or graphs on national and subnational hepatitis B vaccination coverage (HepB3 and HepB-BD), and a report on the prevalence of HBV infection (indicated by HBsAg) among children. The biomarker survey report should detail the survey’s objectives, methods (including sampling methods, sample size assumptions, and laboratory testing procedures), and results (including HBsAg prevalence and confidence intervals by age, gender, geographic region, and other demographic factors). If available, data on antenatal HBV testing coverage and HBsAg prevalence should also be included, particularly for countries without universal birth dose vaccination. Any additional supporting documents or optional data may be submitted, along with a discussion of data limitations. To initiate the verification process, countries must contact the WHO Regional Office’s Immunization and Vaccine Unit and submit a formal letter of interest from the national health administration to the Regional Director of WHO. This letter should include the name and contact information of the designated country representative for the verification process. A team of three experts from the Verification Expert Panel (VEP) will review the submitted verification package. The country contact person must be available to address any clarifications requested by the panel. The VEP will communicate its decision to the Regional Director, who will inform the country of the outcome. Countries must provide detailed information on their immunization systems, policies, and hepatitis B control measures. This includes data on live births, the percentage of births in health facilities, the percentage of births attended by skilled practitioners, and primary school enrollment rates. Information on universal hepatitis B vaccination schedules, including the timing of the birth dose and subsequent doses, should be provided. If catch-up vaccination programs are implemented, details on the target age groups, years of implementation, and coverage rates must be included. Subnational data on HepB birth dose and HepB3 coverage for the past 3–5 years should also be submitted, along with explanations for any coverage rates below 80% at the subnational level or 90% at the national level. Countries must report on hepatitis B vaccination coverage among high-risk groups, such as healthcare workers and other vulnerable populations (e.g., people who inject drugs, sex workers). If universal or selective testing of pregnant women for HBsAg is implemented, data on testing coverage and HBsAg prevalence among pregnant women for at least three years should be provided. For countries without universal newborn vaccination, data on timely HepB birth dose coverage and completed vaccination series among high-risk newborns should be included. Additional services to prevent perinatal transmission of HBV, such as the administration of hepatitis B immunoglobulin to high-risk newborns and antiviral treatment for pregnant women, should be documented. Any other relevant information, including measures to ensure blood and injection safety, may also be submitted. For biomarker surveys assessing HBsAg prevalence among cohorts born after the introduction of universal hepatitis B vaccination, countries must provide detailed survey data. This includes the survey year, geographic scope, sampling base, survey design, and hepatitis B virus markers tested. Information on the test kits used (e.g., ELISA or rapid tests) and their brands must also be specified.
